before_results.readmission: The positive class is a patient being readmitted within 30 days. Missing a readmission is the worse mistake for patient safety, because that patient goes home without any extra follow up. However, flagging too many patients would overload the discharge staff, so I would accept a moderate threshold instead of flagging everyone.
before_results.diabetes: The positive class is a doctor diagnosis or an HbA1c of 6.5% or more. Missing a positive case is the worse mistake here too. An undiagnosed adult goes untreated, while a false alarm only costs one extra follow up test. The team wants a sensitivity of at least 0.90.

recommendations.readmission: None of the models is good enough to use as a decision tool. All four rank patients poorly, with test AUROC between 0.58 and 0.65, and at a threshold of 0.50 they flag almost no one, about 0.1 per 100 patients. If the team still wants a prompt for extra follow up, I would pick logistic regression at a threshold of 0.10. It does about as well as the others on test patients and doesn't just memorize the training patients, with an AUROC of 0.66 on training and 0.64 on test. It flags about 26 out of every 100 patients and catches 44% of readmissions. However, only about 15% of the patients it flags actually come back, so most of the flags are false alarms. Random forest looks the best on training patients at 0.997, but that doesn't carry over to new patients.
recommendations.diabetes: I would use logistic regression at a threshold of 0.12. It has the highest test AUROC at 0.827 and shows no sign of memorizing, since training AUROC was 0.81. At 0.12 it reaches 90% sensitivity, which is 180 of the 200 test patients with diabetes. The tradeoff is that it flags about 52 out of every 100 adults, and about 35 of those are false alarms, so only 33% of flagged adults actually have diabetes. I picked that threshold by looking at the test patients, so sensitivity on new adults will probably come in a little below 90%. Random forest and gradient boosting both memorized the training patients, with a training AUROC of about 0.99 and a test AUROC between 0.81 and 0.82.

design.design_choice: I put the per 100 numbers next to the threshold slider, showing how many patients get flagged and how many are false alarms. For diabetes I also added a button that jumps to the highest threshold that still reaches 0.90 sensitivity. The clinical lead has to staff the follow up tests, so they need to see the costs to hit the target in real adults, not just percentages.
design.ai_turned_down: I used Claude Code to write the models module and the app, and I did not turn down any of its suggestions.
